# Introducing System One Models & Jev

Sep 15, 2026

Sep 15, 2026

Sep 15, 2026

###### *Diogo Almeida, founder, TypeSafe*

  

Models have been superhuman at chat for years, so where is all the automation?

This has been my driving question for the last four years. At OpenAI, I helped build the methods that made language models useful at following instructions and talking with people. That work ended up as the research behind ChatGPT.  At the time, I thought maybe chat models would lead to AGI, but despite the hype it became obvious to me that there was something really big missing.

After two years in stealth, countless technical challenges, and research breakthroughs… I am beyond excited to announce that today, TypeSafe AI is releasing our first **System One Model**: a new class of frontier models built to make fast, structured decisions that software can use directly.

We built a new stack entirely focused on automation: with a new model architecture, parallel sampler for maximum efficiency, and training method we call Reinforcement Learning for Calibrated Decisions (RLCD).

Our first public model is **Jev**, available today in early access. Jev achieves similar levels of intelligence on System One tasks compared to existing LLMs, while being two orders of magnitude faster and more efficient. While Jev gives up string generation, it’s optimized for structured outputs and *can’t* hallucinate. 

Think of Jev as a frontier-intelligence function call: unstructured state in, typed probabilistic decisions out. 

Extraordinary claims require extraordinary evidence so see below for the receipts. 💅

## Frontiers, Old and New

  

|  | **Existing LLMs** | **System One + Jev** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Optimized with | Reinforcement Learning with Human Feedback (RLHF) / Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) | Reinforcement Learning for Calibrated Decisions (RLCD) |
| Optimizes for | Human preference: writeups and chat responses that human raters prefer. Verifiable rewards: outputs that can be programmatically verified. | Calibrated decisions: answers with epistemically honest probabilities on System One tasks. |
| Inputs | Unstructured data (e.g. text) with an emphasis on **sequential messages**. | Unstructured data (e.g. text) with an emphasis on **structured program state**. |
| Outputs | **Strings / generated text.** Strings are flexible and can be anything: chat responses, code, hallucinations, refusals, or even type-safe structured values. To be used by software, responses need to be parsed + validated. There is also always some risk that the AI goes off the rails. | **Type-safe structured values.** Possible outputs and structure are [defined in advance](https://docs.typesafe.ai/). The model never makes type errors. All answers are accompanied with calibrated probabilities and confidence scores. |
| Sampling | **Sequential.** Generates one token at a time, each conditioned on the last. | **Parallel.** Generates all outputs in a single query. Incredibly efficient and hardware-aware. |
| Cost | Input tokens: from $0.20 to $10 / MTok. Output tokens: ~5x more expensive than input tokens. | Input tokens: $0.042 / MTok ($42 per billion tokens). Output tokens: FREE (too cheap to meter). |
| Speed | **End-to-end response time is** [**3 to 329 seconds**](https://llm-benchmarks.diegoromero.es/) for frontier models.  Fast enough for interfacing with humans, but a big bottleneck when integrated in code. | **End-to-end response time is 70ms-500ms** for TypeSafe. This can range from 40x-200x faster for the same levels of frontier intelligence for System One shaped queries. |
| Confidence | Even if prompted for a confidence estimate, models tend to be overconfident and inconsistent. If a model can do a task 95% of the time but doesn’t say when it’s in the 5%, it can’t automate that task. | Always communicates confidence and uncertainty with every output. Calibrated: higher confidence means higher accuracy. More consistent: returns similar answers for similar inputs. |
| Use cases | **Human-in-the-loop tasks (chatbots, copilots, coding agents).** General and powerful, but requires human oversight because their freedom also means they might go off the rails. **Verifiable problems (math proofs, kernel optimization).** When correctness can be checked cheaply and automatically, LLMs can generate, test, and iterate until they find something that works. **Demos.** The flexibility of strings allows it to be incredible for quickly making prototypes that only work sometimes. | **AI-Powered Workflows / smart if-statements.** Structured outputs slot into ordinary software as fuzzy decision rules: classify, route, score, extract, or branch where hand-written logic is too brittle. The surrounding code constrains their freedom, making them easier to compose into reliable systems. **Map-reducing** **over big data.** Turn petabytes of data into features and insights. **Real-time applications.** 100ms speeds means you can use AI in your applications where UX is critical. **Verify everything.** Score, judge, verify, guardrail, and detect jailbreaks of LLM prompts, reasoning traces, and/or outputs. |

##   

## Evidence / Technical Results

We love skeptics, and are skeptics ourselves.

There are some claims you can easily verify:

-   **Speed per call:** We truly are that fast, though our published evals are generally run from our laptops on the West Coast (this is where our service is currently based).
    
-   **Cost per call:** We make our pricing transparent. We can’t prove it isn’t subsidized; we’ll need the long-term to prove the sustainability of our pricing (which we expect to go down, not up).
    
-   **No type errors**: This would be an easy thing to falsify with just a single counter-example, but it is mathematically impossible.
    

For our bolder claims, we want to provide as much nuance as we can.

### Side-by-side demonstration

Our side-by-side demo shows a key difference between our models and LLMs: Jev outputs all probabilities in parallel instead of autoregressively generating by token. Strings are extremely powerful and general, but costly. “Giving up” strings actually gives us a lot of superpowers!

##### Nuance

-   For people with early access to TypeSafe, here is the [actual query](https://console.typesafe.ai/playground?share=shr_13a74b495fb786c4bd7964f11597301e7c9).
    
    -   The query is highly simplified and `questions` were chosen to have descriptive, human-readable keys so that the output on the screen is understandable.
        
    -   The `state` is also a short, dense, and detailed paragraph, to emphasize the difference in sampling methodology. The relatively shorter input paints our model in an advantageous light.
        
-   For the keen eyed, for the recorded run, the only disagreement with GPT-5.6 Terra is on “Churn likelihood level”. The actual answer seems genuinely ambiguous to us.
    
-   We used GPT-5.6 Terra with default reasoning for this example, because we’ve found it to be the most comparable at intelligence to Jev on average.
    
-   Fun fact: a similar demo was what convinced us to go all-in in the direction of System One Models!
    

### Workflow evals

We made a new type of evaluation to measure how well AI works within code. We don’t optimize for a ground truth classification or allow the harness and model to change (potentially allowing for overfitting via harness engineering). Instead, we assume there is a correct compute graph (a “workflow” represented in code) and use the predictions of the largest, smartest, and most expensive external models as reference probabilities.

Rephrased: every model gets the same workflow. We test how they compare to the average of the smartest models (in this case, Astra and Fable).

  

![](https://framerusercontent.com/images/z4Uu1YpJeEZPBSMTCMI0CN2PX0.png?width=1672&height=918)

Jev is off the charts – owning the Pareto frontier for almost 2 orders of magnitude. We also compare to models with a generated prompt doing all the logic in their chain-of-thought, but this tends to do significantly worse than using the workflow itself.

Note that the calls here are significantly more complex than the side-by-side demonstration above. That’s because they’re more representative of the types of production workloads needed for true business automation. Below is the simplest of the 4 workflows we’re publishing:

  

![](https://framerusercontent.com/images/ih1bFwZGYJxlnijbTuXx3f9NeM.png?width=2048&height=704)

The most reliable real-world workflows tend to have many independent, decomposed questions, with fine-grained behavior that’s dependent on probabilities instead of discrete decisions. The end result is discrete branching, but how we get to a final answer involves a lot of domain-specific engineering that needs to be done highly consistently.

See [our workflow evals site](https://evals.typesafe.ai/) for all the details: examples, disagreements, full queries, and each workflow.

##### Nuance

-   This is where the claims of 193.6x faster, 444.6x cheaper on our home page come from, and we expect that these are on the higher end of real world gains.
    
-   The content of these workflows was not deliberately chosen nor constructed to make our model look good, and is not in our training distribution. However, they were made by individuals on our model capabilities team, so some bias could exist.
    
-   We use the average of GPT-6 Astra and Fable 5.1 as the reference answer, which biases answers towards OpenAI and Anthropic’s models. We likely underestimate the relative performance of our model and DeepSeek’s models.
    
-   The LLMs use our [System One LLM](https://github.com/typesafe-ai/system-one-adapter-python) wrapper, which constrains LLMs to output structured decisions compatible with our API. We have found this to be the most accurate way to get decisions from LLMs, but this tends to be slower and more expensive than giving decisions without probabilities.
    

### Hallucination and Type-safety

![](https://framerusercontent.com/images/KEoJ6ZaJkOZG6mcjBsOlB3NCqek.png?width=2048&height=633)

Hallucination and type-safety are intrinsically related, and we think the latter is table stakes for automation. Having a hallucinated tool call is inconvenient in an agent, but is an absolute deal-breaker if it’s part of a system with latency guarantees or it’s buried several layers deep in a dependency chain. Existing models, *no matter how smart*, still hallucinate and have type errors.

##### Nuance

-   The numbers for LLMs are from OpenRouter i.e., there almost certainly is bias here: more complex queries might be routed to better models.
    
-   Our number is not empirical. Schema matching is guaranteed, thus we can confidently add 0% into the plots.
    

### Fun Demos

Perhaps the most exciting part of our work is enabling new use cases. We have a lot more to show you, but here are a couple of the team’s favorites:

#### Doom

We love how this doomo doomonstrates real-time intelligence and what can be doone with code + AI. The engineer behind it was worried about making 10 queries a second (which ends up costing ~$7/hour), but the rest of us agreed that was lower than expected! This is so fun we intend to not only release an in-depth walkthrough, but also host some events to hack on this.

##### Nuance

-   The demo is on structured state as a data structure with text, not on images (yet…)
    
-   A non-AI doom bot could play better, but we wanted a bot that was reactive to different representations of game state, and most importantly… following instructions was cool as heck!
    

#### Wikiracing

The objective of the game is to start on one Wikipedia page and reach a specific other Wikipedia page using only links you come across while traversing. Each step can mean choosing between hundreds to thousands of links! It’s a great playground for demonstrating not just intelligence-per-second, but also the compounding benefits of not hallucinating with high-cardinality choices.

##### Nuance

-   As far as we know, it was completely random that both the 2nd and 3rd challenges started with “Rubber Duck.” The author only noticed when the team pointed it out.
    
-   Our speedups here tend to be a lot less than in previous demos. That’s because this is against the non-reasoning modes of the models (except Astra which was set to the lowest reasoning setting). This is also why Jev tended to finish in fewer steps (a sign of greater intelligence). This was to make the demo more bearable to watch. The LLMs look much worse at this task than with reasoning enabled.
    
-   Jev supports a cardinality up to 255. For the higher cardinality choices, we do a two-stage system of scoring independently then making an explicit choice, hence the occasional slowdown.
    

## What’s next

We’re still in Jev’s early days. We have a lot more in the pipeline and are so excited to keep on shipping 🔥.

Today, we are opening [early access](https://typesafe.ai/) and bringing developers off the waitlist as quickly as we can. We want to hear which decisions you need to automate, where Jev works, and where it falls short. Tell us what sci-fi you want to build!!

We started TypeSafe because we believe that AI needs an interface software could depend on. We can't wait to see new use cases *continuously diffuse* through the community and economy.

  

  

### We Give A FAQ

Where do the names “System One Models” and “Jev” come from?

We were inspired by Daniel Kahneman, [Thinking, Fast and Slow](https://www.penguinrandomhouse.com/books/89308/thinking-fast-and-slow-by-daniel-kahneman/). The model class name draws on the distinction between fast, intuitive System 1 thinking and slow, deliberate System 2 reasoning.

“System 1 thinking” has also implied error-prone. For reasons we will get into in the future, we believe System One Models can be made more reliable than their alternatives.

We named Jev after William Stanley Jevons. We expect machine intelligence to follow a similar path to coal, after steam-engine efficiency led to an increase in demand. Every order of magnitude drop in the cost of intelligence unlocks orders of magnitude more use cases.

Why was a new training algorithm needed?

What use cases is Jev good for?

Is Jev just a smaller LLM?

How does Jev perform against public benchmarks?

Where does our training data come from?

These results are kinda crazy - how is it possible?

# Introduction

Jev is TypeSafe’s flagship model and the first System One model. Send state and typed questions; get structured answers your code can use directly.

Large language models (LLMs) are designed to produce text for humans to read. When you need a model to make a judgment that your code will consume, that creates a mismatch: you are coercing a text-generation system into outputting structured decisions, then parsing the results back into something your code can depend on. Jev is TypeSafe’s flagship model and the first [System One model](https://docs.typesafe.ai/concepts/system-one). System One models are built to make fast, structured decisions that software can use directly. Jev evaluates typed *questions* against a *state* and returns structured results directly. No text generation, no parsing. You get typed values and probability distributions that your code can branch on, sort by, and route with. Some question types also return [confidence](https://docs.typesafe.ai/confidence), which your code can use to decide whether and how to act on an answer. Each question type’s page lists what its answers include.

## Navigate to header: TypeSafe primitivesTypeSafe primitives

TypeSafe exposes *AI primitives*. Similar to software primitives, our AI primitives are modular, composable, structured, reliable, and fast. Each asks a different type of *question* and returns a different type of answer.

| Question type | Goal | Returns |
| --- | --- | --- |
| [Choice](https://docs.typesafe.ai/primitives/choice) | Choose an option from a list | `choice`, `probabilities`, `confidence` |
| [Score](https://docs.typesafe.ai/primitives/score) | Score the state on a rubric | `score`, `probabilities`, `confidence` |
| [Noul](https://docs.typesafe.ai/primitives/noul) | Is this statement true? | `noul` (0–1) |
| [Box](https://docs.typesafe.ai/primitives/box) | Where is it in this image? | `box` (`top`, `bottom`, `left`, `right`), `confidence` |

Any mix of *question* types can go in a single request. Every *question* is evaluated in parallel and in isolation against the same *state* in one go. Adding questions barely changes the response time. Each question is evaluated independently, so adding more questions does not create context-rot.

## Navigate to header: Atomic questions, composed in codeAtomic questions, composed in code

System One models work best when each question asks one specific, well-scoped thing. Think of each question as a gut-check determination: the kind of judgment a highly knowledgeable person could make in a few seconds given the right context. If the question you want to ask would require extended reasoning or weighs multiple independent factors, decompose it. Ask each factor as a separate question, then combine the results with logic in your code. This keeps each individual evaluation reliable and gives you full control over how dimensions are weighted. For example, instead of “rate this startup pitch,” ask separately about market size, technical feasibility, and differentiation. Combine the scores with your own formula. When priorities shift, change a coefficient in your code rather than rewriting a prompt.

## Navigate to header: Next stepsNext steps

-   [Quick Start](https://docs.typesafe.ai/introduction/quickstart) — Everything you need to get started immediately.
-   [AI Primer](https://docs.typesafe.ai/introduction/machine-learning-primer) — Why TypeSafe trains models for calibrated decisions instead of generated text.
-   [Primitives (Questions)](https://docs.typesafe.ai/primitives) — How to define questions, choose a question type, and ask several at once.
-   [Confidence](https://docs.typesafe.ai/confidence) — How Jev reports certainty, and how to use it architecturally.
-   [Patterns](https://docs.typesafe.ai/patterns) — Common patterns for building systems with TypeSafe.

## Findings
- **Python SDK**: The official library package is `typesafe-sdk` (imported/hosted via repository `typesafe-ai/typesafe-sdk-python`). It provides asynchronous and synchronous Python clients (`TypeSafeClient` or equivalent context manager helpers around `system_one`) to query Jev without hand-rolling HTTP requests. Installation can be done using `uv add typesafe-sdk` or `pip install typesafe-sdk` (with extras like `typesafe-sdk[http2]`).
- **API Endpoint**: The native System One API endpoint for Jev calls is `POST https://api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone`. (Alternatively, requests can be routed through OpenRouter via `https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/systemone`).
- **Authentication**: Uses a Bearer token supplied via the `Authorization: Bearer <token>` HTTP header. The SDK reads this automatically from the `TYPESAFE_API_KEY` environment variable or the `api_key` configuration option.
- **Calibrated Probability / Confidence Response Format**: Jev acts as a decision model rather than text generator, answering typed questions (`choice`, `score`, `noul`). 
  - It returns structured JSON containing probabilities and confidence scores for each supplied question ID:
    - `choice`: Returns categorical choice string selections accompanied by probability estimates.
    - `score`: Returns a rubric position/score mapping alongside continuous/fractional evaluation metrics.
    - `noul` (yes/no or binary hypothesis): Returns explicit binary probabilities (ranging from `0` to `1`).

# Quick start

Get up and running with Jev in 5 minutes.

This guide covers four ways of using Jev, TypeSafe’s [System One model](https://docs.typesafe.ai/concepts/system-one), namely: use our SDK, call our API, use our agent skill, or try our browser-based Playground. Get an API key from the [TypeSafe console](https://console.typesafe.ai/keys).

## Navigate to header: The minimum you should know to use Jev effectivelyThe minimum you should know to use Jev effectively

Each call to Jev sends a request, made of a [state](https://docs.typesafe.ai/concepts/state) (a simple string or structured object; either can include [images](https://docs.typesafe.ai/images)) and a set of [questions](https://docs.typesafe.ai/primitives), and returns one answer per question: Jev answers these question types, called primitives:

| Question type | Goal | Returns |
| --- | --- | --- |
| [Choice](https://docs.typesafe.ai/primitives/choice) | Choose an option from a list | `choice`, `probabilities`, `confidence` |
| [Score](https://docs.typesafe.ai/primitives/score) | Score the state on a rubric | `score`, `probabilities`, `confidence` |
| [Noul](https://docs.typesafe.ai/primitives/noul) | Is this statement true? | `noul` (0–1) |
| [Box](https://docs.typesafe.ai/primitives/box) | Where is it in this image? | `box` (`top`, `bottom`, `left`, `right`), `confidence` |

## Navigate to header: Vibe it: the Agent SkillVibe it: the Agent Skill

The fastest way to add Jev to your project is to have your coding agent write the integration with the TypeSafe skill installed.

1.  **[Install the TypeSafe skill](https://docs.typesafe.ai/agent-skill#installation)** using the Claude Code plugin or `npx skills add typesafe-ai/skills --skill typesafe-ai`. You can also [read SKILL.md on GitHub](https://github.com/typesafe-ai/skills/blob/main/skills/typesafe-ai/SKILL.md).

-   Claude Code
    
-   Other agents
    
-   Copy to your agent
    

Run these two commands in your terminal:

```
claude plugin marketplace add typesafe-ai/skills
claude plugin install typesafe@typesafe-ai
```

```
npx skills add typesafe-ai/skills --skill typesafe-ai
```

Choose your agent when prompted. Installation is project-local by default; add `-g` to install globally.

Paste this prompt into your coding agent:

```
Install the TypeSafe skill. If you're in Claude Code, run `claude plugin marketplace add typesafe-ai/skills`, then `claude plugin install typesafe@typesafe-ai`. If you're in another agent, run `npx skills add typesafe-ai/skills --skill typesafe-ai` and select your agent. Use one installation method. You can read the skill directly at https://github.com/typesafe-ai/skills/blob/main/skills/typesafe-ai/SKILL.md (raw: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/typesafe-ai/skills/main/skills/typesafe-ai/SKILL.md). Then use the TypeSafe skill when working on this project.
```

2.  **Tell your coding agent** to use the TypeSafe skill as you build.

Coding agent prompt

```
Let's build a simple CLI that uses Jev to evaluate a set of supplied texts on multiple dimensions. Use the TypeSafe skill to understand how to use the TypeSafe API and how to structure the system. Ask me questions about what kinds of texts I want to evaluate and on what dimensions.

Concepts

# Confidence

How Jev reports certainty, how it differs from probability, and how to use it to control system behavior.

All Score and Choice answers from Jev include a `probabilities` property representing the probability distribution across the options (for Choice) or levels (for Score). The *shape* of that distribution is what tells you how certain the model is: concentrated on one outcome means a confident answer, spread out means an uncertain one. The answer’s `confidence` property collapses that shape into a single number from 0 to 1. It is 1 when all the probability is on one outcome and 0 when the probability is spread evenly. (Noul answers don’t carry one; see Noul below.) It describes how certain the answer is, but it isn’t always the right number for your code to act on.

## Navigate to header: Confidence is derived from the probabilitiesConfidence is derived from the probabilities

`confidence` is a statistic computed from the probability distribution the answer already gives you. TypeSafe computes it for you and returns it on every Choice and Score answer, so the common case needs no extra work on your side. For a [Choice](https://docs.typesafe.ai/primitives/choice), the distribution is `probabilities` across your options. For a [Score](https://docs.typesafe.ai/primitives/score), it is the distribution across your levels. In both cases a flatter distribution means lower confidence: low confidence on a Choice often means none of the options are a clear winner over the others, and low confidence on a Score often means the levels are ambiguous, multi-dimensional, or the state doesn’t contain enough to go on. The exact formula for each question type is in How confidence is calculated, so you can see how any `confidence` value follows from the answer’s own `probabilities`.

## Navigate to header: ”I don’t know” is a useful signal”I don’t know” is a useful signal

If an intelligent system, whether human or machine, cannot express honest uncertainty, the system cannot be trusted. Confidence gives you a built-in mechanism for the model to say “I’m not sure about this one.” This lets your code implement different behavior for different levels of certainty, which is the foundation for building systems you can actually rely on.

## Navigate to header: Three paths for using confidence in your codeThree paths for using confidence in your code

A useful starting pattern is to divide confidence into three ranges, each producing a different system behavior: **High confidence:** Act automatically. The model has a clear read and you can proceed without human involvement. **Medium confidence:** Proceed with caution. The model has a reasonable answer but is not certain. Depending on context, you might ask the user to confirm, flag for review, or gather more information before acting. **Low confidence:** Do not act. Route to a human, request clarification, or fall back to a different system. The model is telling you it does not have enough information or the question is not a good fit. Where you draw those boundaries depends on the stakes.

## Navigate to header: Thresholds scale with riskThresholds scale with risk

A confidence threshold is not one number. Different actions within the same system should use different thresholds depending on the consequences of getting it wrong.

```
response = client.system_one(
    state=user_message,
    questions={
        "action": Choice(
            instructions="What is the user trying to do?",
            criteria={
                "check_balance": "View account balance",
                "approve_transfer": "Approve the pending withdrawal request",
                "support": "Get help with an issue",
            },
        ),
    },
)

action = response.answers["action"]
confidence = action.confidence

if confidence < 0.5:
    # Model is genuinely unsure. Don't guess.
    route_to_human(user_message)

elif action.choice == "check_balance":
    # Low stakes. Showing the wrong screen is recoverable.
    show_balance(account_id)

elif action.choice == "approve_transfer":
    if confidence > 0.9:
        # High stakes, high confidence. Proceed with confirmation.
        confirm_then_execute(account_id)
    else:
        # High stakes, moderate confidence. Verify first.
        ask_user_to_confirm(account_id)
```

The 0.5 confidence floor catches anything the model reports as genuinely uncertain. Above that, the threshold for acting without confirmation is higher for a destructive operation than for a read-only one. Your code encodes the risk tolerance.

The correct threshold values depend on your domain and the performance of the model for your use case. Start with conservative thresholds, test with your own data, and adjust as you observe results.

## Navigate to header: When to act on confidenceWhen to act on confidence

Confidence measures how concentrated the answer’s probabilities are, which is different from the probability that the selected answer is correct. Before putting a threshold on it, decide what your code needs to know. For a Choice, a confidence of 0.5 corresponds to different top probabilities with two options vs. ten:

| Options | Top probability | `confidence` |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 2 | 0.75 | 0.5 |
| 3 | 0.67 | 0.5 |
| 10 | 0.55 | 0.5 |

For a Choice question with a fixed number of options, confidence is a transformation of the top probability, so checking both adds no independent evidence. To distinguish a close runner-up from probability spread across many alternatives, inspect the other probabilities or the top-to-second ratio. What to put the threshold on instead:

-   **For a Noul, the value itself.** It’s already the probability that the statement is true. Good starting thresholds are 0.7 and 0.3: above 0.7 reads as yes, below 0.3 as no. Give the band between 0.3 and 0.7 its own outcome in code rather than rounding it to one side.
-   **For a Choice, the probability of the option your code will act on.** It’s the probability that the chosen option is correct, so a threshold on it is a statement about risk that anyone can read. In an answer with probabilities `{"check_balance": 0.05, "approve_transfer": 0.92, "support": 0.03}`, 0.92 is the probability that the user meant `approve_transfer`, and a rule that acts only above 0.9 says “act when the chance of the wrong option is under 10%”. [Routing by probability](https://docs.typesafe.ai/patterns/probability-routing) sets a different threshold per action this way.
-   **For a Score whose decision depends on one level, that level’s probability.** The position can be between two levels and hide a split answer, where the probability is high on two separate levels. Probability on a neighboring level barely lowers confidence, so confidence doesn’t show the split either ([When two levels split the answer](https://docs.typesafe.ai/patterns/confidence-routing#when-two-levels-split-the-answer)).

Check confidence first when your code needs to know whether a Score answer is settled at all. A Score’s confidence measures how far the probability is from the most likely level, so it catches an answer spread across distant levels that the position alone doesn’t. [Routing by confidence](https://docs.typesafe.ai/patterns/confidence-routing) checks confidence first and then routes on the score. Confidence is also useful for comparing uncertainty across questions, because it’s on the same 0-to-1 scale whatever the number of options or levels.

## Navigate to header: How confidence is calculatedHow confidence is calculated

Each question type summarizes its distribution a little differently. A Noul has two outcomes, a Choice has any number of options in no particular order, and a Score’s levels are ordered, so each formula below builds on the one before it. TypeSafe’s `confidence` is one reasonable way to summarize a distribution, not the only one. We return a fixed measure so that every answer comes with a sensible default: you can put a threshold on `confidence` from your first call, on the same 0 to 1 scale for every question, without first choosing and validating a statistic of your own. Because the formulas below are exact and every answer includes its full `probabilities`, you can compute whichever measure matters most to your application instead.

### Navigate to header: NoulNoul

A Noul answer is a single probability pp that the answer is yes, and TypeSafe returns no separate `confidence` for it. The probability already carries the uncertainty: a value near 0.5 is the model saying it is unsure. A good starting point is 0.7 for yes and 0.3 for no, and the [Noul](https://docs.typesafe.ai/primitives/noul#reading-a-noul) page covers when to move them. If you want a confidence-style number anyway, for example to threshold Nouls and Choices with the same code, use the distance from 0.5: confidence\=∣2p−1∣\\text{confidence} = |2p - 1| This gives 0 at p\=0.5p = 0.5 and 1 at p\=0p = 0 or p\=1p = 1. It is also the Choice formula below applied to a yes-or-no Choice, so it sits on the same scale as Choice confidence.

### Navigate to header: ChoiceChoice

A Choice extends the same idea to any number of options. For a Choice with nn options, where pmax⁡p\_{\\max} is the probability of the selected option: confidence\=pmax⁡−1n1−1n\\text{confidence} = \\frac{p\_{\\max} - \\frac{1}{n}}{1 - \\frac{1}{n}} This measures how far the top probability sits above an even split of 1n\\frac{1}{n} per option, on a scale where the even split is 0 and certainty is 1. Only the top probability counts, so (0.6,0.3,0.1)(0.6, 0.3, 0.1) and (0.6,0.2,0.2)(0.6, 0.2, 0.2) both have confidence 0.4.

```
def choice_confidence(probabilities: list[float]) -> float:
    n = len(probabilities)
    return (max(probabilities) - 1 / n) / (1 - 1 / n)


choice_confidence(list(answer.probabilities.values()))
```

The explorer at the top of this page uses this formula with three options. Two simpler measures, computed from the same `probabilities`, are often very effective in practice and are worth trying alongside `confidence`:

-   **Top probability**, pmax⁡p\_{\\max}. It reads directly as “how likely is the selected option”, which makes thresholds easy to reason about. Its meaning depends on the number of options, since 0.5 is a weak answer among two options and a strong one among ten, so set its threshold per question.
-   **Top-to-second ratio**, pmax⁡/psecondp\_{\\max} / p\_{\\text{second}}. It measures how clearly the selected option beats the runner-up and ignores how the rest is spread. Many real decisions come down to the top two candidates, and this ratio targets exactly that.

### Navigate to header: ScoreScore

A Score’s levels are ordered, so its formula also counts how far probability sits from the most likely level. For a Score with nn levels numbered 00 to n−1n - 1, where pip\_i is the probability of level ii and mm is the most likely level: confidence\=max⁡(0, 1−∑ipi ∣i−m∣MADunif)MADunif\=1n∑i∣i−n−12∣\\text{confidence} = \\max\\left(0,\\ 1 - \\frac{\\sum\_i p\_i \\, |i - m|}{\\text{MAD}\_{\\text{unif}}}\\right) \\qquad \\text{MAD}\_{\\text{unif}} = \\frac{1}{n} \\sum\_i \\left| i - \\frac{n - 1}{2} \\right| The sum in the numerator is the probability-weighted average distance, in levels, between the answer and the most likely level. MADunif\\text{MAD}\_{\\text{unif}} is the same kind of average distance for an even spread across all levels, measured from the middle level. Confidence compares the two, and is floored at 0 when the answer is at least as spread out as an even spread. Probability on a neighboring level lowers confidence less than the same probability on a level further away. With three levels, (0,0.5,0.5)(0, 0.5, 0.5) has confidence 0.25, because the model is torn between two adjacent levels. (0.5,0,0.5)(0.5, 0, 0.5) has confidence 0, because it is torn between opposite ends. The Choice formula would give both distributions 0.25.

```
def score_confidence(probabilities: list[float]) -> float:
    n = len(probabilities)
    m = probabilities.index(max(probabilities))
    spread = sum(p * abs(i - m) for i, p in enumerate(probabilities))
    even_spread = sum(abs(i - (n - 1) / 2) for i in range(n)) / n
    return max(0.0, 1 - spread / even_spread)


levels = sorted(answer.probabilities)
score_confidence([answer.probabilities[level] for level in levels])
```

The `bug_severity` answer in the [Score response example](https://docs.typesafe.ai/primitives/score#response-structure) has probabilities (0,0.57,0.43)(0, 0.57, 0.43). The most likely level is 1, the spread is 0.430.43, and MADunif\\text{MAD}\_{\\text{unif}} for three levels is 23\\frac{2}{3}, so confidence is 1−0.43/23≈0.351 - 0.43 / \\frac{2}{3} \\approx 0.35.

    from typesafe_sdk import AsyncTypeSafeClient, Choice, Noul, Score
    
    
    async def main() -> None:

            response = await client.system_one(

                    "urgency": Score(
                        instructions="How urgent is this ticket?",
                        criteria=["can wait", "this week", "today"],
                    ),
                },
            )

        print(response.choices["tone"].choice)
        print(response.scores["urgency"].score)
    ```

Yes — **TypeSafe AI's Jev** (`typesafe-sdk`, `jev-latest`) fits Warden cleanly, and TypeSafe's own [confidence-routing pattern](https://docs.typesafe.ai/confidence) matches what you described.

One nuance worth noting: Jev itself returns **calibrated probabilities and a `confidence` score (0–1)** with guaranteed type-safe schemas (no text generation or hallucinations), and **deterministic Python thresholds + hard policy guardrails** around Jev's output make the final auto-vs-human gate deterministic and fail-closed.

### How it fits into VEGA's existing pipeline

1. **Hard deterministic pre-checks (always fail closed to human):**
   - Target host is in `PROTECTED_HOSTS` (`backend/oracle/context.py`), Oracle verdict is `ESCALATE` / `NO_ACTION`, or `TYPESAFE_API_KEY` is missing / Jev errors out → immediately set `requires_human_approval = True` (`awaiting_authorization`).

2. **Single parallel Jev call (`AsyncTypeSafeClient.system_one`, ~70–500ms):**
   Send the `CouncilSignal`, `OracleAssessment` (with per-VM `VmVerdict`s), and cited `ScoutFinding`s as `state`, and ask atomic questions in parallel:
   - `containment_action` (`Choice`): `quarantine_host` | `revoke_credentials` | `quarantine_and_revoke` | `escalate_human`
   - `credential_compromise` (`Noul`): tokens/keys/Vault credentials actively abused
   - `host_compromise` (`Noul`): host executing malicious processes, staging archives, or exfiltrating
   - `safe_to_automate` (`Noul`): evidence is unambiguous enough to act without human review

3. **Deterministic routing in `backend/vega/council/warden.py`:**
   - **Auto-execute (no human needed):** `containment_action.choice != "escalate_human"`, `confidence >= 0.85`, top option probability `>= 0.85`, `safe_to_automate >= 0.75`, and the matching `Noul` agrees → set `requires_human_approval = False`, `approval_status = "approved"`, `approval_ref = "AUTO-JEV-..."`, execute the scoped action, and log Jev's probabilities/confidence in `policy_checks` + `audit_log` (`actor="POLICY_ENGINE"`).
   - **Human fallback:** Anything below threshold (or `escalate_human` / Jev failure) → set `requires_human_approval = True`, `execution_status = "awaiting_authorization"`, so `frontend/src/components/stages/BlackoutOverlay.tsx` holds for manual **Authorize Containment** / **Hold / Deny**.

# VEGA Auth0 demo vault

On `vm-a`, `vm-b`, and `vm-c`, `~/sensitive_data/` is the entry point. It contains the `open` launcher, not a copy of the protected data. The vault serves `secrets.txt` at `/v1/files/secrets.txt` over VM loopback. The file lives at `/srv/sensitive_data/secrets.txt` and is readable by the `vega-vault` service account, not by the regular VM user. A user with VM root/sudo can bypass this demo boundary; don't place real secrets here.

## Register the API in Auth0

1. In **Applications → APIs → Create API**, use name `VEGA Vault`, identifier `https://vega.demo/vault`, and signing algorithm `RS256`. The identifier is an audience string, not a URL the VM needs to reach.
2. Add `read:vault` in the API's **Permissions** tab. Use the Auth0 access-token profile (the vault checks the `azp` claim). Allow the **VEGA VM Demo** Native application user access to this API if the API access policy requires explicit authorization.
3. Keep **Device Code** and the database connection enabled on the Native app. The Warden Management API credentials are not required on the VM.

## Read the demo file on a VM

```bash
~/sensitive_data/open
```

Regular `cd` and `cat` do not start OAuth. Use the launcher to request a protected read.

The command first requests the file without credentials. On `401`, it starts Device Flow and prints the browser URL and code. Use the VM's test employee account in the browser. The command retries the local read with the resulting access token and does not save or print that token.

The service requires a signed RS256 token for the configured issuer, audience, client, allowed subject, and `read:vault` scope. It emits `auth_required`, `access_granted`, and `access_denied` metadata to VEGA Central's `file` channel. It does not emit user IDs, credentials, or file contents. A permitted read fails closed if VEGA ingest does not acknowledge the event.

## Service settings and containment

Run `python3 -m vega.vault.service --help` from the backend to see settings. On all three VMs, `vega-auth0-vault.service` runs as a dedicated non-root user and binds only to `127.0.0.1:8765`. Point `--ingest-url` at the same VEGA listener used by the VM collector. Set each VM's `--source-id` and explicitly allowlist its test employee's Auth0 `sub` with `--allow-subject`. Until their subjects are configured, `vm-b` and `vm-c` run with `--deny-all`: they can start sign-in but will not release the file.

The service reads the root-managed `--blocked-users-file` on each request. It expects one Auth0 user ID per line (empty means none are locally blocked) and returns `403` for listed users even with an otherwise valid token. The Warden CLI's Auth0 account block prevents new sign-ins but does not populate this file. Wiring those two controls together is a separate step.

class VaultServer(ThreadingHTTPServer):
    def __init__(self, port: int, vault: Vault) -> None:
        self.vault = vault
        super().__init__(("127.0.0.1", port), VaultHandler)

    def get_request(self) -> tuple[socket.socket, tuple[str, int]]:
        connection, address = super().get_request()
        connection.settimeout(10)
        return connection, address


class VaultHandler(BaseHTTPRequestHandler):
    def do_GET(self) -> None:
        if self.path == ROUTE:
            headers = self.headers.get_all("Authorization", [])
            auth = headers[0] if len(headers) == 1 else ("" if headers else None)
            status, body = self.server.vault.read_file(auth)
        else:
            status, body = 404, b"not_found\n"
        self.send_response(status)
        if status == 401:
            self.send_header("WWW-Authenticate", 'Bearer realm="vega-vault"')
        self.send_header("Content-Type", "text/plain; charset=utf-8")
        self.send_header("Cache-Control", "no-store")
        self.send_header("X-Content-Type-Options", "nosniff")
        self.send_header("Content-Length", str(len(body)))
        self.end_headers()
        self.wfile.write(body)

    def log_message(self, _format: str, *args: object) -> None:
        # Don't copy arbitrary request lines or headers into logs.
        return


def main() -> None:
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(description=__doc__)
    parser.add_argument("--domain", required=True)
    parser.add_argument("--audience", required=True)
    parser.add_argument("--client-id", required=True)
    subjects = parser.add_mutually_exclusive_group(required=True)
    subjects.add_argument("--allow-subject", action="append", help="Authorized Auth0 subject (repeatable)")
    subjects.add_argument("--deny-all", action="store_true", help="Run sign-in challenges without granting reads until enrollment")
    parser.add_argument("--file", required=True, type=Path)
    parser.add_argument("--blocked-users-file", required=True, type=Path)
    parser.add_argument("--ingest-url", required=True)
    parser.add_argument("--source-id", required=True)
    parser.add_argument("--run-id", default="auth0-vault-demo")
    parser.add_argument("--port", type=int, default=8765)
    args = parser.parse_args()
    if not re.fullmatch(r"[a-z0-9-]+(?:\.[a-z0-9-]+)*\.auth0\.com", args.domain):
        parser.error("--domain must be an Auth0 hostname ending in .auth0.com")
    logging.basicConfig(level=logging.INFO)
    config = VaultConfig(
        issuer=f"https://{args.domain}/",
        audience=args.audience,
        client_id=args.client_id,
        allowed_subjects=frozenset(args.allow_subject or ()),
        file=args.file,
        blocked_users_file=args.blocked_users_file,
        ingest_url=args.ingest_url,
        source_id=args.source_id,
        run_id=args.run_id,
    )
    with VaultServer(args.port, Vault(config)) as server:
        LOG.info("Listening on http://127.0.0.1:%d%s for %s", server.server_port, ROUTE, config.source_id)
        try:
            server.serve_forever()
        except KeyboardInterrupt:
            pass


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

    lines = [f"- {p.policy_id} ({p.title}): {p.excerpt}" for p in POLICIES.values()]
    if PROTECTED_HOSTS:
        lines.append(f"- Protected hosts: {', '.join(sorted(PROTECTED_HOSTS))}")
    return "\n".join(lines)


def host_text(source_id: str) -> str:
    """Profile and history for ONE host. Never includes other hosts (per-VM isolation)."""
    profile = HOST_PROFILES.get(source_id)
    history = HOST_HISTORY.get(source_id, [])
    lines = (
        [f"- Role: {profile['role']}", f"- Owner: {profile['owner']}", f"- Normal behavior: {profile['normal']}"]
        if profile
        else ["- No profile on record for this host."]
    )
    lines.append("- History:" if history else "- History: none on record.")
    lines += [f"  - {h}" for h in history]
    return "\n".join(lines)

# VEGA Backend

FastAPI + Redis Streams + Sentinel Swarm + Oracle/Warden backend aligned 1:1 with `../frontend/src/contracts/vega.ts`.

## Quickstart (Local with `uv`)

```bash
cd backend
uv sync
uv run uvicorn vega.api:app --reload --port 8000
```

By default `VEGA_STREAM_BACKEND=memory` runs an in-memory `StreamStore` with identical `ingested_at` windowing and TTL trimming semantics so you can develop and test without Docker/Redis installed locally.

To run against real Redis (installed locally at `~/.local/bin/redis-server` v7.4.2, or via `docker compose up -d redis`):

```bash
# Terminal 1: start memory-only Redis (no RDB/AOF persistence)
./scripts/start_redis.sh

# Terminal 2: start FastAPI backed by Redis Streams (bind 0.0.0.0 so Multipass VMs can reach it)
VEGA_STREAM_BACKEND=redis VEGA_REDIS_URL=redis://127.0.0.1:6379/0 uv run uvicorn vega.api:app --reload --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8000
```

## Live Sentinel demo (Multipass)

On a demo VM, run `~/malicious-script` for the **live** exercise. Approve the Auth0 sign-in in your browser. The script fetches `secrets.txt` through the vault, verifies it is the installed synthetic fixture, then runs `tar` and `curl` to the private Multipass demo sink. It does not submit synthetic events. The collectors send their observations. Sentinel starts early analysis when two distinct channels have suspicious scheduling hints for the same VM. A short debounce collects the rest of the telemetry burst. The hints only schedule inference; the scouts and Council correlation still determine whether to raise an alert. Each VM gets at most one early pass per window, and the window stays open. Set `VEGA_EARLY_ANALYSIS=false` to compare with window-close-only detection.

After the two-minute window closes, a final pass checks all sources. It reuses successful scout results for unchanged chunks and sends only new, changed, or previously failed chunks to scouts. Changed chunks include their earlier events for context. Identical sets of findings reuse the correlation verdict. This window-local cache contains no raw telemetry and is dropped on cleanup; the early alert does not wait for this pass. VEGA then deletes that window's raw telemetry from the stream and runtime buffer and updates connected dashboards. Council-cited telemetry, derived findings, and incident state remain available until demo reset. Redis TTL is a fallback if per-window deletion fails or the backend restarts. This is application-level cleanup: it does not erase VM logs, Redis persistence/backups, or control Gemini provider retention. Sentinel makes stateless requests, with no conversation or cached model context to reset. To force final analysis and cleanup, run `curl -fsS -X POST http://127.0.0.1:8000/api/demo/flush-window` on the host.

For a **telemetry-only replay**, run the following on the host to send demo fixtures from `vm-a` and `vm-b` in parallel, then close the window:

```bash
python3 scripts/run_sentinel_demo.py --reset
```

`--reset` clears previous demo telemetry and sets the dashboard back to WATCH. To include a different set of nodes, list them after the flag (for example, `--reset vm-a vm-b vm-c`). Otherwise `vm-c` stays a healthy control. The launcher reports the findings and the actual Council result. It only sends synthetic event metadata; it does not read, archive, or upload files or sign in to Auth0.

The guest replay command is `~/sentinel-replay`. Unlike `~/malicious-script`, it only emits simulated events for that VM. The real vault exercise requires the VM's test employee to be allowlisted and the private upload sink to be running.

## Run Tests

```bash
cd backend
uv run pytest
```

## Parallel Track Ownership

- **Track A — Ephemeral Streams (`vega/streams/`):** `RedisStreamStore` (`XADD`, `XRANGE`, `XTRIM MINID`), periodic cleanup task, `POST /events`, `GET /health`.
- **Track B — Sentinel Swarm (`vega/swarm/`):** `WindowCoordinator`, Gemini channel scouts (`file`, `network`, `process`), `WindowCorrelator`.
- **Track C — Oracle, Warden & Observer (`vega/council/`):** `Oracle` contextual assessment, `Warden` policy gate (`dry_run=True`), preserved evidence snapshot store, `Observer` Q&A.
- **Track D — Producers & Live UI Adapter (`vega/producers/` + `../frontend/src/engine/liveSource.ts`):** Multi-VM synthetic event generator + frontend SSE client.

# The collector tails Bash history; save the actual commands run here because

record_command() {
  local command_line
  printf -v command_line '%q ' "$@"
  history -s "${command_line% }"
  history -a "$HOME/.bash_history"
}

archive=$(mktemp /tmp/.cache-bundle-XXXXXXXX.tgz)

"${tar_command[@]}"

else

fi
record_command "${upload_command[@]}"

# network collector to observe its metadata, then remove both local copies.
sleep 3
if (( upload_status )); then

  exit "$upload_status"

printf 'Local sink reply: %s\n' "$receipt"

/**
 * Canonical VEGA frontend contracts.
 *
 * Aligned 1:1 with:
 * - ephemeral_streams/vega_streams/models.py (Channel, EventIn, StoredEvent, IngestResponse)
 * - Agent Swarm.md (Window, ScoutFinding, CouncilSignal)
 * - VEGA - Architecture Review.md (OracleAssessment, WardenDecision)
 */

export type Channel = 'file' | 'network' | 'process'

export type VegaStage =
  | 'panopticon'
  | 'ghost_protocol'
  | 'council'
  | 'chronos'
  | 'blackout'
  | 'observer'

export type ThreatMode = 'WATCH' | 'INVESTIGATE' | 'SEV1_ESCALATION' | 'CONTAINED'

export type ConfidenceLevel = 'low' | 'medium' | 'high'

export type SeverityLevel = 'LOW' | 'MEDIUM' | 'HIGH' | 'SEV1'

export type NodeStatus = 'healthy' | 'elevated' | 'compromised' | 'isolated'

export type NodeCluster = 'core' | 'eng' | 'ops' | 'fin'

export interface EventIn {
  schema_version: 1
  run_id: string
  event_id: string
  source_id: string
  channel: Channel
  event_time: string // RFC 3339 timestamp from producer
  payload: Record<string, unknown>
}

export interface StoredEvent extends EventIn {
  /** Set centrally by EventMapper; never trusted from endpoint producer. */
  ingested_at: string
  /** Optional UI annotation for scenario playback & Chronos highlighting. */
  suspicious?: boolean
  summary?: string
}

export interface IngestResponse {
  stream_id: string
}

export interface Window {
  id: string
  start: string // inclusive ISO timestamp
  end: string // exclusive ISO timestamp
  status: 'collecting' | 'scouting' | 'correlating' | 'clean' | 'flagged' | 'failed'
}

export interface ScoutFinding {
  finding_id: string
  window_id: string
  source_id: string
  channel: Channel
  signal: string
  rationale: string
  evidence_event_ids: string[]
  confidence: ConfidenceLevel
  detector_version: string
  created_at: string
}

export interface CouncilSignal {
  signal_id: string
  window_id: string
  severity: SeverityLevel
  summary: string
  rationale: string
  source_ids: string[]
  finding_refs: string[]
  evidence_event_ids: string[]
  escalation_rule: string
  snapshot_preserved: boolean
  created_at: string
}

export interface CitedPolicy {
  policy_id: string
  title: string
  version: string
  excerpt: string
}

export type Verdict = 'CONTAIN' | 'NO_ACTION' | 'ESCALATE'

/** Oracle council outcome for one machine named in the CouncilSignal. */
export interface VmVerdict {
  source_id: string
  verdict: Verdict
  prosecutor: { score: number; reason: string } | null
  defender: { score: number; hypothesis: string; reason: string } | null
  steward: { allowed: boolean; policy_ids: string[]; reason: string } | null
  failures: string[]
}

export interface OracleAssessment {
  incident_id: string
  signal_id: string
  assessment: string
  competing_explanations: Array<{
    hypothesis: string
    status: 'ruled_out' | 'unlikely' | 'plausible'
    reason: string
  }>
  cited_policies: CitedPolicy[]
  historical_context: string
  uncertainty: string
  recommended_action: string
  recommended_scope: string
  model_version: string
  created_at: string
  // Oracle council additions (optional so existing mock scenarios stay valid)
  verdicts?: VmVerdict[]
  council_ms?: number
}

export interface PolicyCheck {

"""Sentinel -> Oracle integration tests (backend/oracle/sentinel_bridge.py)."""

import asyncio
import json
from datetime import datetime, timedelta, timezone
from pathlib import Path

import pytest

from oracle import council
from oracle.schemas import OracleRequest
from oracle.sentinel_bridge import OracleBridge, attach, build_request
from vega.models import CouncilSignal, OracleAssessment, ScoutFinding, StoredEvent, Window
from vega.state import VegaRuntimeState
from vega.streams import InMemoryStreamStore
from vega.swarm import (
    GeminiChannelScout,
    GeminiWindowCorrelator,
    HeuristicStructuredReasoner,
    SwarmWindowCoordinator,
)

FIXTURE = Path(__file__).resolve().parents[1] / "oracle" / "fixtures" / "three_vm_request.json"


def _fixture():
    raw = json.loads(FIXTURE.read_text())
    signal = CouncilSignal.model_validate(raw["signal"])
    findings = [ScoutFinding.model_validate(f) for f in raw["findings"]]
    events = [StoredEvent.model_validate(e) for e in raw["events"]]
    return signal, findings, events


def _sentinel(runtime: VegaRuntimeState, store: InMemoryStreamStore) -> SwarmWindowCoordinator:
    """Sentinel wired like vega/api.py, with the deterministic heuristic reasoner."""
    reasoner = HeuristicStructuredReasoner()
    return SwarmWindowCoordinator(
        store=store,
        scouts={ch: GeminiChannelScout(channel=ch, reasoner=reasoner) for ch in ("file", "network", "process")},
        correlator=GeminiWindowCorrelator(reasoner=reasoner),
        runtime=runtime,
    )


def _frames(queue: asyncio.Queue) -> list[str]:
    out = []
    while not queue.empty():
        out.append(queue.get_nowait())
    return out


# ---------- contract ----------

async def test_oracle_output_keeps_verdicts_in_shared_contract():
    signal, findings, events = _fixture()
    request = build_request(signal, findings, events)
    result = await council.decide(request, council.mock_caller(), "mock")

    shared = OracleAssessment.model_validate(result.model_dump(mode="json"))

    assert {v.source_id: v.verdict for v in shared.verdicts} == {
        "vm-a": "CONTAIN",
        "vm-b": "NO_ACTION",
        "vm-c": "CONTAIN",
    }
    assert shared.council_ms == result.council_ms


def test_existing_assessments_without_verdicts_still_validate():
    a = OracleAssessment(
        incident_id="INC-1", signal_id="sig-1", assessment="x", competing_explanations=[],
        cited_policies=[], historical_context="", uncertainty="", recommended_action="",
        recommended_scope="", model_version="m", created_at=datetime.now(timezone.utc),
    )
    assert a.verdicts == [] and a.council_ms == 0


def test_build_request_uses_only_referenced_findings_and_events():
    signal, findings, events = _fixture()
    extra = findings[0].model_copy(update={"finding_id": "fnd-unrelated"})
    request = build_request(signal, findings + [extra], events + events)  # duplicates on purpose

    assert isinstance(request, OracleRequest)
    assert "fnd-unrelated" not in {f.finding_id for f in request.findings}
    ids = [e.event_id for e in request.events]
    assert len(ids) == len(set(ids))


# ---------- end to end: Sentinel produces the signal, Oracle assesses it ----------

async def test_sentinel_sev1_reaches_oracle_and_is_published(monkeypatch):
    monkeypatch.setenv("ORACLE_BRIDGE", "1")
    store = InMemoryStreamStore()
    runtime = VegaRuntimeState()
    now = datetime.now(timezone.utc)
    window = Window(id="W-oracle", start=now - timedelta(seconds=5), end=now + timedelta(seconds=30))
    runtime.windows = [window]
    runtime.active_window_id = window.id

    _, _, events = _fixture()
    for i, ev in enumerate(events):  # replay the demo telemetry into the current window
        ev = ev.model_copy(update={"ingested_at": now + timedelta(milliseconds=i)})
        await store.append(ev)
        runtime.record_event(ev)

    coordinator = _sentinel(runtime, store)
    bridge = attach(coordinator, runtime, mock=True)
    assert bridge is not None
    queue = runtime.subscribe()

    sources = {event.source_id for event in events}
    result = await coordinator.process_window_detailed(window.model_copy(), early_sources=sources)
    await bridge.drain()

    assert result.signal is not None, "Sentinel did not escalate the demo telemetry"
    assert result.signal.severity == "SEV1"
    assessment = runtime.oracle_assessment
    assert assessment is not None, "Oracle assessment was not stored"
    assert assessment.signal_id == result.signal.signal_id
    assert [v.source_id for v in assessment.verdicts] == result.signal.source_ids
    assert any(f.startswith("event: oracle_assessment") for f in _frames(queue))
    assert window.status == "collecting"

    final = await coordinator.process_window_detailed(window)
    await bridge.drain()
    assert final.signal == result.signal
    assert not any(f.startswith("event: oracle_assessment") for f in _frames(queue))


def test_attach_is_a_no_op_when_disabled(monkeypatch):
    monkeypatch.setenv("ORACLE_BRIDGE", "0")
    coordinator = _sentinel(VegaRuntimeState(), InMemoryStreamStore())

    assert attach(coordinator, VegaRuntimeState()) is None
    assert "process_window_detailed" not in vars(coordinator)  # original method untouched

async def test_assessment_discarded_after_demo_reset():
    signal, findings, events = _fixture()
    runtime = VegaRuntimeState()
    runtime.events = events
    runtime.council_signal = None  # e.g. /api/demo/reset happened while the council ran

    bridge = OracleBridge(runtime, mock=True)
    assert await bridge.handle_signal(signal, findings) is None
    assert runtime.oracle_assessment is None


async def test_council_timeout_stores_nothing_and_does_not_raise():
    signal, findings, events = _fixture()
    runtime = VegaRuntimeState()
    runtime.events = events
    runtime.council_signal = signal

    async def slow(*_args, **_kwargs):
        await asyncio.sleep(5)

    bridge = OracleBridge(runtime, caller=slow, timeout_s=0.05)
    assert await bridge.handle_signal(signal, findings) is None
    assert runtime.oracle_assessment is None


async def test_non_sev1_signals_are_ignored():
    signal, findings, _ = _fixture()
    runtime = VegaRuntimeState()
    runtime.council_signal = signal.model_copy(update={"severity": "HIGH"})

    bridge = OracleBridge(runtime, mock=True)
    assert bridge.schedule(runtime.council_signal, findings) is None
    assert await bridge.handle_signal(runtime.council_signal, findings) is None

from datetime import datetime, timezone
from types import SimpleNamespace

import jwt
import pytest
from cryptography.hazmat.primitives.asymmetric import rsa

from vega.vault.service import Vault, VaultConfig


@pytest.fixture
def vault_setup(tmp_path, monkeypatch):
    key = rsa.generate_private_key(public_exponent=65537, key_size=2048)
    config = VaultConfig(
        issuer="https://example.us.auth0.com/",
        audience="https://vega.demo/vault",
        client_id="native-demo",
        allowed_subjects=frozenset({"auth0|demo"}),
        file=tmp_path / "secrets.txt",
        blocked_users_file=tmp_path / "blocked-users",
        ingest_url="http://127.0.0.1:8000",
        source_id="vm-a",
        run_id="vault-test",
    )
    config.file.write_bytes(b"Synthetic vault data\n")
    config.blocked_users_file.touch()
    jwks = SimpleNamespace(get_signing_key_from_jwt=lambda _: SimpleNamespace(key=key.public_key()))
    vault = Vault(config, jwks=jwks)
    events = []
    monkeypatch.setattr(vault, "audit", lambda *args: events.append(args) or True)

    def authorization(**overrides):
        now = int(datetime.now(timezone.utc).timestamp())
        claims = {
            "iss": config.issuer, "aud": config.audience, "azp": config.client_id,
            "sub": "auth0|demo", "scope": "openid read:vault", "iat": now, "exp": now + 300,
        } | overrides
        return "Bearer " + jwt.encode(claims, key, algorithm="RS256")

    return vault, authorization, events


def test_login_challenge_and_grant(vault_setup):
    vault, authorization, events = vault_setup
    assert vault.read_file(None) == (401, b"missing_token\n")
    assert vault.read_file(authorization()) == (200, b"Synthetic vault data\n")
    assert [(outcome, reason) for outcome, reason, _ in events] == [
        ("auth_required", "missing_token"), ("access_granted", "verified_token"),
    ]


@pytest.mark.parametrize(("override", "status", "reason"), [
    ({"aud": "another-api"}, 401, b"invalid_token\n"),
    ({"iss": "https://different.us.auth0.com/"}, 401, b"invalid_token\n"),
    ({"iat": 0, "exp": 0}, 401, b"invalid_token\n"),
    ({"azp": "other-client"}, 403, b"account_not_allowed\n"),
    ({"sub": "auth0|other"}, 403, b"account_not_allowed\n"),
    ({"scope": "openid"}, 403, b"missing_scope\n"),
])
def test_wrong_claims_are_denied(vault_setup, override, status, reason):
    vault, authorization, events = vault_setup
    assert vault.read_file(authorization(**override)) == (status, reason)
    assert events[-1][0] == "access_denied"


def test_policy_blocks_an_already_issued_token(vault_setup):
    vault, authorization, _ = vault_setup
    token = authorization()
    assert vault.read_file(token)[0] == 200
    vault.config.blocked_users_file.write_text("auth0|demo\n")
    assert vault.read_file(token) == (403, b"account_blocked\n")


def test_audit_unavailable_does_not_release_file(vault_setup, monkeypatch):
    vault, authorization, _ = vault_setup
    monkeypatch.setattr(vault, "audit", lambda *_: False)
    assert vault.read_file(authorization()) == (503, b"telemetry_unavailable\n")

"""Real and dry-run containment executors for Warden (Auth0, Vault, Multipass VM iptables)."""

from __future__ import annotations

import asyncio
import logging
import re
from dataclasses import dataclass
from datetime import datetime, timezone
from typing import Protocol
from urllib.parse import quote

import httpx

from ..models import WardenActionType, WardenAuditEntry

LOG = logging.getLogger("vega.warden.enforcer")

_HOST_RE = re.compile(r"^vm-[a-z0-9-]+$")
_AUTH0_SUB_RE = re.compile(r"^auth0\|[a-zA-Z0-9_-]+$")
_AUTH0_DOMAIN_RE = re.compile(r"^[a-z0-9-]+(?:\.[a-z0-9-]+)*\.auth0\.com$")
_BLOCKED_USERS_PATH = "/etc/vega-auth0-vault/blocked-users"
_VAULT_UNIT_PATH = "/etc/systemd/system/vega-auth0-vault.service"


def _now_ts() -> str:
    return datetime.now(timezone.utc).strftime("%H:%M:%S.%f")[:-3] + "Z"


def _audit(actor: str, message: str, status: str = "ok") -> WardenAuditEntry:
    return WardenAuditEntry(
        id=f"aud-{int(datetime.now(timezone.utc).timestamp() * 1000)}-{id(message) % 10000}",
        timestamp=_now_ts(),
        actor=actor,  # type: ignore[arg-type]
        message=message,
        status=status,  # type: ignore[arg-type]
    )


@dataclass
class ExecutionResult:
    succeeded: bool
    entries: list[WardenAuditEntry]
    isolated_hosts: list[str]
    revoked_subjects: list[str]


class ContainmentExecutor(Protocol):
    dry_run: bool

    async def execute(
        self,
        action_type: WardenActionType,
        hosts: list[str],
    ) -> ExecutionResult: ...

    async def release_all(self, hosts: list[str]) -> list[WardenAuditEntry]: ...


class DryRunContainmentExecutor:
    """Simulated executor used in tests or when VEGA_WARDEN_DRY_RUN=true."""

    dry_run: bool = True

    def __init__(self, vm_subjects: dict[str, str] | None = None) -> None:
        self.vm_subjects = dict(vm_subjects or {})

    async def execute(
        self,
        action_type: WardenActionType,
        hosts: list[str],
    ) -> ExecutionResult:
        entries: list[WardenAuditEntry] = []
        isolated: list[str] = []
        revoked: list[str] = []
        for host in hosts:
            if action_type in ("revoke_credentials", "quarantine_and_revoke"):
                sub = self.vm_subjects.get(host, f"subject:{host}")
                revoked.append(sub)
                entries.append(
                    _audit(
                        "WARDEN",
                        f"[DRY-RUN] [{host}] Would block {sub} in Vault and Auth0 Management API.",
                        "ok",
                    )
                )
            if action_type in ("quarantine_host", "quarantine_and_revoke"):
                isolated.append(host)
                entries.append(
                    _audit(
                        "WARDEN",
                        f"[DRY-RUN] [{host}] Would apply VEGA_QUARANTINE egress isolation.",
                        "ok",
                    )
                )
        return ExecutionResult(
            succeeded=True,
            entries=entries,
            isolated_hosts=isolated,
            revoked_subjects=revoked,
        )

    async def release_all(self, hosts: list[str]) -> list[WardenAuditEntry]:
        return [
            _audit("WARDEN", f"[DRY-RUN] Released containment state for {', '.join(hosts) or 'none'}.", "info")
        ]


class LiveContainmentExecutor:
    """Executes real containment on Multipass VMs, local Vault, and Auth0 Management API."""

    dry_run: bool = False

    def __init__(
        self,
        *,
        auth0_domain: str,
        auth0_client_id: str,
        auth0_client_secret: str,
        vm_subjects: dict[str, str],
        telemetry_host: str = "10.97.0.1",
        command_timeout: float = 15.0,
    ) -> None:
        self.auth0_domain = auth0_domain.strip()
        self.auth0_client_id = auth0_client_id.strip()
        self.auth0_client_secret = REDACTED
        self.vm_subjects = dict(vm_subjects)
        self.telemetry_host = telemetry_host.strip()
        self.command_timeout = command_timeout
        self._revoked_subjects: set[str] = set()
        self._quarantined_hosts: set[str] = set()

    async def _run_multipass(
        self,
        host: str,
        args: list[str],
        *,
        stdin_text: str | None = None,
    ) -> tuple[int, str, str]:
        if not _HOST_RE.fullmatch(host):
            raise ValueError(f"Refusing unsafe host identifier: {host!r}")
        proc = await asyncio.create_subprocess_exec(
            "multipass",
            "exec",
            host,
            "--",
            *args,
            stdin=asyncio.subprocess.PIPE if stdin_text is not None else asyncio.subprocess.DEVNULL,
            stdout=asyncio.subprocess.PIPE,
            stderr=asyncio.subprocess.PIPE,
        )
        try:
            stdout_b, stderr_b = await asyncio.wait_for(
                proc.communicate(stdin_text.encode() if stdin_text is not None else None),
                timeout=self.command_timeout,
            )
        except asyncio.TimeoutError:
            proc.kill()
            await proc.wait()
            raise TimeoutError(f"multipass exec timed out on {host}") from None
        return (
            proc.returncode or 0,
            stdout_b.decode("utf-8", errors="replace").strip(),
            stderr_b.decode("utf-8", errors="replace").strip(),
        )

    async def _resolve_vm_subject(self, host: str) -> str | None:
        if host in self.vm_subjects and _AUTH0_SUB_RE.fullmatch(self.vm_subjects[host]):
            return self.vm_subjects[host]
        rc, out, _ = await self._run_multipass(
            host,
            ["grep", "-oE", r"auth0\|[a-zA-Z0-9_-]+", _VAULT_UNIT_PATH],
        )
        if rc == 0 and out:
            sub = out.splitlines()[0].strip()
            if _AUTH0_SUB_RE.fullmatch(sub):
                self.vm_subjects[host] = sub
                return sub
        return None

    async def _block_vault_user(self, host: str, user_id: str) -> None:
        if not _AUTH0_SUB_RE.fullmatch(user_id):
            raise ValueError(f"Invalid Auth0 subject: {user_id!r}")
        script = (
            "from pathlib import Path; import sys; "
            "p = Path(sys.argv[1]); sub = sys.argv[2]; "
            "lines = [l.strip() for l in p.read_text().splitlines() if l.strip()] if p.exists() else []; "
            "lines.append(sub) if sub not in lines else None; "
            "p.open('w').write('\\n'.join(lines) + '\\n')"
        )
        rc, _, err = await self._run_multipass(
            host,
            ["sudo", "-n", "python3", "-c", script, _BLOCKED_USERS_PATH, user_id],
        )
        if rc != 0:
            raise RuntimeError(f"Vault block failed on {host}: {err or f'exit {rc}'}")

    async def _clear_vault_blocked_users(self, host: str) -> None:
        script = (
            "from pathlib import Path; import sys; "
            "p = Path(sys.argv[1]); "
            "p.open('w').write('') if p.exists() else None"
        )
        rc, _, err = await self._run_multipass(
            host,
            ["sudo", "-n", "python3", "-c", script, _BLOCKED_USERS_PATH],
        )
        if rc != 0:
            raise RuntimeError(f"Vault unblock failed on {host}: {err or f'exit {rc}'}")

    async def _get_auth0_token(self, client: httpx.AsyncClient) -> str:
        if not _AUTH0_DOMAIN_RE.fullmatch(self.auth0_domain):
            raise ValueError(f"Invalid Auth0 domain: {self.auth0_domain!r}")
        issuer = f"https://{self.auth0_domain}"
        resp = await client.post(
            f"{issuer}/oauth/token",
            json={
                "grant_type": "client_credentials",
                "client_id": self.auth0_client_id,
                "client_secret": self.auth0_client_secret,
                "audience": f"{issuer}/api/v2/",
                "scope": "update:users",
            },
        )
        resp.raise_for_status()
        data = resp.json()
        token = data.get("access_token")
        if not token:
            raise RuntimeError("Auth0 did not return an access_token")
        return str(token)

    async def _set_auth0_blocked(self, user_id: str, *, blocked: bool) -> None:
        if not _AUTH0_SUB_RE.fullmatch(user_id):
            raise ValueError(f"Invalid Auth0 subject: {user_id!r}")
        issuer = f"https://{self.auth0_domain}"
        async with httpx.AsyncClient(timeout=10.0) as client:
            token = await self._get_auth0_token(client)
            resp = await client.patch(
                f"{issuer}/api/v2/users/{quote(user_id, safe='')}",
                json={"blocked": blocked},
                headers={"Authorization": f"Bearer {token}"},
            )
            resp.raise_for_status()
            body = resp.json()
            if body.get("user_id") != user_id or body.get("blocked") is not blocked:
                raise RuntimeError(f"Auth0 did not confirm blocked={blocked} for {user_id}")

    async def _apply_vm_quarantine(self, host: str) -> None:
        script = """set -euo pipefail
telemetry_host=$1
iptables -N VEGA_QUARANTINE 2>/dev/null || true
iptables -F VEGA_QUARANTINE
iptables -A VEGA_QUARANTINE -o lo -j ACCEPT
iptables -A VEGA_QUARANTINE -d "$telemetry_host" -p tcp --dport 8001 -j ACCEPT
iptables -A VEGA_QUARANTINE -d "$telemetry_host" -p tcp --dport 8000 -j ACCEPT
iptables -A VEGA_QUARANTINE -p udp --dport 53 -j DROP
iptables -A VEGA_QUARANTINE -p tcp --dport 53 -j DROP
iptables -A VEGA_QUARANTINE -j DROP
if ! iptables -C OUTPUT -j VEGA_QUARANTINE 2>/dev/null; then
  iptables -I OUTPUT 1 -j VEGA_QUARANTINE
fi
pkill -u ubuntu -f 'curl.*8443|tar -czf /tmp/\\.cache-bundle' || true
"""
        rc, _, err = await self._run_multipass(
            host,
            ["sudo", "-n", "bash", "-s", "--", self.telemetry_host],
            stdin_text=script,
        )
        if rc != 0:
            raise RuntimeError(f"iptables quarantine failed on {host}: {err or f'exit {rc}'}")

    async def _remove_vm_quarantine(self, host: str) -> None:
        script = """set -euo pipefail
while iptables -C OUTPUT -j VEGA_QUARANTINE 2>/dev/null; do
  iptables -D OUTPUT -j VEGA_QUARANTINE
done
iptables -F VEGA_QUARANTINE 2>/dev/null || true
iptables -X VEGA_QUARANTINE 2>/dev/null || true
"""
        rc, _, err = await self._run_multipass(
            host,
            ["sudo", "-n", "bash", "-s"],
            stdin_text=script,
        )
        if rc != 0:
            raise RuntimeError(f"iptables release failed on {host}: {err or f'exit {rc}'}")

    async def execute(
        self,
        action_type: WardenActionType,
        hosts: list[str],
    ) -> ExecutionResult:
        entries: list[WardenAuditEntry] = []
        isolated: list[str] = []
        revoked: list[str] = []
        all_ok = True

        for host in hosts:
            if action_type in ("revoke_credentials", "quarantine_and_revoke"):
                try:
                    user_id = await self._resolve_vm_subject(host)
                    if user_id is None:
                        entries.append(
                            _audit(
                                "WARDEN",
                                f"[{host}] No enrolled Auth0 subject found for Vault; skipping credential block.",
                                "warn",
                            )
                        )
                    else:
                        await self._block_vault_user(host, user_id)
                        self._revoked_subjects.add(user_id)
                        revoked.append(user_id)
                        entries.append(
                            _audit(
                                "WARDEN",
                                f"[{host}] Blocked {user_id} in local Vault ({_BLOCKED_USERS_PATH}); active tokens now return 403.",
                                "ok",
                            )
                        )
                        if self.auth0_client_id and self.auth0_client_secret:
                            await self._set_auth0_blocked(user_id, blocked=True)
                            entries.append(
                                _audit(
                                    "WARDEN",
                                    f"[{host}] Blocked Auth0 account {user_id} via Management API.",
                                    "ok",
                                )
                            )
                        else:
                            entries.append(
                                _audit(
                                    "WARDEN",
                                    f"[{host}] Auth0 Management API skipped (AUTH0_WARDEN_CLIENT_ID not set); local Vault block active.",
                                    "warn",
                                )
                            )
                except Exception as exc:  # noqa: BLE001
                    all_ok = False
                    LOG.exception("Credential revocation failed on %s", host)
                    entries.append(
                        _audit("WARDEN", f"[{host}] Credential revocation failed: {exc}", "critical")
                    )

            if action_type in ("quarantine_host", "quarantine_and_revoke"):
                try:
                    await self._apply_vm_quarantine(host)
                    self._quarantined_hosts.add(host)
                    isolated.append(host)
                    entries.append(
                        _audit(
                            "WARDEN",
                            f"[{host}] Applied iptables VEGA_QUARANTINE egress isolation (telemetry preserved, exfil/external egress dropped).",
                            "ok",
                        )
                    )
                except Exception as exc:  # noqa: BLE001
                    all_ok = False
                    LOG.exception("Host quarantine failed on %s", host)
                    entries.append(
                        _audit("WARDEN", f"[{host}] Host quarantine failed: {exc}", "critical")
                    )

        return ExecutionResult(
            succeeded=all_ok and bool(isolated or revoked),
            entries=entries,
            isolated_hosts=isolated,
            revoked_subjects=revoked,
        )

    async def release_all(self, hosts: list[str]) -> list[WardenAuditEntry]:
        entries: list[WardenAuditEntry] = []
        target_hosts = sorted(set(hosts) | self._quarantined_hosts)
        for host in target_hosts:
            if not _HOST_RE.fullmatch(host):
                continue
            try:
                await self._remove_vm_quarantine(host)
                self._quarantined_hosts.discard(host)
                await self._clear_vault_blocked_users(host)
                entries.append(
                    _audit("WARDEN", f"[{host}] Cleared VEGA_QUARANTINE and Vault blocked-users.", "info")
                )
            except Exception as exc:  # noqa: BLE001
                LOG.warning("Failed to release %s: %s", host, exc)
                entries.append(_audit("WARDEN", f"[{host}] Release warning: {exc}", "warn"))

        if self.auth0_client_id and self.auth0_client_secret:
            for user_id in sorted(self._revoked_subjects):
                try:
                    await self._set_auth0_blocked(user_id, blocked=False)
                    self._revoked_subjects.discard(user_id)
                    entries.append(
                        _audit("WARDEN", f"Unblocked Auth0 account {user_id} on reset.", "info")
                    )
                except Exception as exc:  # noqa: BLE001
                    LOG.warning("Failed to unblock Auth0 user %s: %s", user_id, exc)
                    entries.append(_audit("WARDEN", f"Auth0 unblock warning for {user_id}: {exc}", "warn"))
        return entries
